transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-04
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Alex Carter (Redwood AE), Nina Patel (Redwood SE), Maya (CTO Peregrine), Samir (Staff SWE), Priya (SRE), Jules (PM), Liam (Data)

Summary:
Quick hosted-api walkthough focusing on chat/text generation basics: streaming behavior, tunable params (temperature/top_p/max_tokens/stop), retry and backoff strategies, idempotency token patterns, console bits for Optimize suggestions. Customer asked about latency vs cost tradeoffs and private data concerns, wanted an actionable recovery playbook and sandbox to run a proof of concept.

Topics covered:
- Streaming vs synchronous calls and when to use each
- Parameter effects on determinism and token usage
- Retry/backoff and idempotency patterns for at-least-once token billing concerns
- Console Optimize recommendations (batching, KV cache, quantization hints)
- Fallbacks to smaller models during capacity pressure
- Basic security questions (SOC2, KMS, retention)

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone thanks for joining, i see most folks are here, maya, samir, priya, thanks for taking the time. we'll kick off with a short walkthrough of the hosted API chat + a hands-on failure-recovery lab, then q and a. nina will show some console/optimize tips mid-call.

[00:22] Maya: thanks alex, our timeline is pretty tight — we want to ship chat responses in our checkout help widget by end of q4. latency is our big worry, also cost, and data residency a bit.

[00:38] Alex: got it. quick qual — do you expect mostly short prompts (under 200 tokens) or long context windows?

[00:46] Samir: mostly short, like 30 to 120 tokens per end-user request, but we do want to pass a small convo history (3–4 messages), and sometimes do small summarizations user-side.

[00:59] Nina: perfect, that's a common pattern for low-latency. we'll demo both streaming and synchronous, but streaming usually is best for perceived latency.

[01:12] Jules: what's the perception difference? do we still pay the same tokens if streaming?

[01:20] Nina: yes you still pay tokens generated. streaming just lets you start showing partial tokens to users as they're produced. think of it as progressive render. same billing, same model.

[01:33] Maya: and retries — if we get a partial stream and then a failure, are we charged twice? this is a big question for finance.

[01:43] Alex: good question — two parts: first, on the API side we recommend using idempotency keys for the request to allow safe retries when the server didn't complete. second, if you got partial tokens in the client, it's tricky — typically you'd detect an incomplete stream and re-issue a request. Redwood's recommend pattern is to use an idempotency token and server-side trimming on retries so you don't double charge for the same utterance. we'll send you the exact snippet.

[02:08] Samir: can you show that snippet now? code example?

[02:12] Nina: yes — here's a pseudo-request: POST /v1/chat with body messages, idempotency_key: uuid, mode: streaming. if you get an error you retry with same key and the backend will either resume or return the final already-completed response. there's also an explicit response flag indicating partial/complete.

[02:36] Priya: does that work with websockets or just http SSE? we likely will use websocket proxying.

[02:44] Nina: both. our streaming supports SSE and websocket transports. the idempotency semantics are transport-agnostic. small caveat: proxies' timeouts can cut streams; we recommend client keepalive and server-side heartbeat.

[03:00] [background murmur]

[03:12] Alex: okay let's do a little live demo — nina, can you share your screen?

[03:19] Nina: sharing now. ok pulling up the console — this is the model selection, we'll pick a mid-sized model for latency tests. you can see the profile: median p95 latencies for 64 tokens at 20ms per token-ish on hosted, those are sample numbers from our catalog.

[03:46] Maya: p95 20ms/token — for us that's maybe 1.2s per 60-token response, sounds reasonable. what's the cost delta to a smaller model?

[03:56] Nina: smaller model reduces token cost by ~35–50% but you trade off quality; some customers run a two-tier approach: default to smaller for common predictable responses and route to larger model for uncertain or escalation cases. Console Optimize suggests that automatically based on a confidence metric.

[04:18] Liam: how do you compute confidence? is that an extra call/score?

[04:24] Nina: we can surface a nll-like score or use a lightweight reranker/embedding lookup to check if the response matches expectations. there is overhead but it's often cheaper than a full-generation. Optimize has a pre-built config to run these checks.

[04:40] Samir: show us parameter tuning — e.g. temperature and top_p — what's best for deterministic answers in checkout flows?

[04:47] Nina: for deterministic help answers use temperature 0 to 0.2 and top_p 0.8–1.0, and set max_tokens conservative (e.g., 80). use stop sequences to avoid trailing disclaimers. That reduces hallucination risk and also controls cost.

[05:09] Maya: will lowering temperature change token count?

[05:13] Nina: it can — lower temperature often produces shorter, more repetitive text, so token counts can go down but not guaranteed. max_tokens is the absolute cap.

[05:24] [00:05:30] Alex: quick note on retry/backoff patterns — exponential backoff with jitter is recommended; if you see 5xx or 429, first try a fast retry for transient networking then backoff. we also surface per-route rate limits.

[05:40] Priya: about 429s, if we get burst load (e.g., 10k qps for a sale) and we have hosted plan, do you have graceful throttling or fallback policies?

[05:52] Nina: yes — hosted has routing tiers; in console you can set a fallback to a cheaper model or to a cached answer. Redwood also supports a degrade-to-stub policy: for high failures, return a short generic message with a handoff to live agent. we'll demo setting a fallback later.

[06:10] Samir: is caching per-prefix possible? we have common checkout prompts.

[06:14] Nina: yes prefix/KV caching works well for chat. console Optimize recommends cache TTLs per prompt pattern; it's automatic for exact-match and approximate for paraphrases via embedding-based keys.

[06:28] Maya: on security: SOC2, KMS, retention — can you summarize?

[06:34] Alex: short summary: yes SOC2 Type II, we support customer-managed keys via KMS integration for Private; for hosted we encrypt at rest with our keys but can enable bring-your-own-key for Dedicated or Private. retention policies are configurable; we can set zero retention for sensitive work. we'll attach the SOC2 pack and the KMS docs.

[06:54] Jules: any difference in audits for sandbox use?

[06:58] Alex: sandbox is a hosted environment but sandbox accounts are still in our audit scope; for production compliance we'd recommend Dedicated or Private if you need stricter control.

[07:10] [00:07:15] Nina: ok switching back to live failure lab — i'm going to simulate a streaming failure and show the recovery pattern. first, normal streaming response — note the partial deltas streaming in.

[07:28] [screen share: console streaming demo]

[07:35] Nina: sending message with idempotency_key = "abc-123" — streaming starts, you see partial tokens like "Sure, here's how to.." then I'm going to drop the stream (simulate a server error).

[07:52] [simulated error appears]

[07:55] Nina: stream closed unexpectedly. client observes incomplete flag. now we'll retry with same idempotency_key. backend recognizes prior attempt incomplete and either resumes or returns final chunk. you avoid a second full charge.

[08:15] Samir: sounds ideal — is that behavior guaranteed across model sizes?

[08:20] Nina: yes across the hosted family. small nuance: if the model switched during the retry (e.g., fallback to smaller), we might return a recomputed shorter response; charge semantics handle that by attributing token usage accordingly, but we document that in billing FAQ.

[08:38] Maya: what about client-side partial display and deduplication — how do we ensure we don't show duplicates after retry?

[08:45] Nina: include delta identifiers in stream messages. when you resume or get the final we reconcile by matching chunk ids. if the final is truncated, you can request the full answer with same key as non-stream to get finalized text.

[09:01] [00:09:10] Alex: next i'll show a simple library snippet we recommend for node/python to handle retry with idempotency, exponential backoff, and token accounting. (gives short code)

[09:21] Samir: can you paste that in chat after the call? we'd like the exact code.

[09:24] Alex: yes will share via repo link.

[09:27] Priya: network/networking — what are the recommend keepalive/timeouts for proxies and load balancers so we avoid false stream kills?

[09:36] Nina: LB idle timeout > 90s recommended for long streams, though for our short responses usually 15–30s is fine. also set TCP keepalive and application-level heartbeats every 10–15s. we'll share a checklist.

[09:50] Maya: let's talk Console Optimize — show the recommendations panel.

[09:55] Nina: here — Optimize scanned your workload (we simulated sample traces) and suggests: lower batch size to minimize latency for small requests, enable KV cache for common prompts, try int8 quantized model for background reranks, and enable model-routing policy to fall back to cheaper model after 2s of queuing.

[10:18] Liam: the quantization suggestion — does that impact accuracy for reranks?

[10:23] Nina: quantized models are slightly lower fidelity but usually fine for scoring/reranking tasks. our console shows historical regression delta so you can decide.

[10:35] [00:10:40] Alex: now a brief Q&A on cost modeling — for sample 30-token input and 60-token output at 100k monthly requests, here's a back-of-envelope of token spend and a suggestion: enable caching and smaller model for 60% of traffic to drop cost by ~40%.

[10:58] Maya: that aligns — finance will want exact numbers; next step to get a quote.

[11:03] Alex: we'll include a throughput-based quote for 10k qps burst and an option for Dedicated capacity.

[11:12] Samir: performance deep dive — would love to run a stress test with you. can we schedule Nina + Priya?

[11:18] Alex: yes — that's in the next steps. nina do you want to propose windows?

[11:22] Nina: i'll propose two windows next week, one for an early smoke test and another for a full stress run. i want to coordinate firewall allowlists ahead.

[11:32] [00:11:40] Samir: let's cover error modes quickly — network blips, 5xx, 429, model OOM. how do we differentiate and respond?

[11:41] Nina: network blips: retry with same idempotency_key after short jitter. 5xx: treat as retryable for a few attempts then failover to fallback policy. 429: respect Retry-After header and backoff; if persistent, route to cached answer. model OOM: we return 503 with specific code and console raises an alert — fallback to smaller model automatically if configured.

[12:02] Priya: for alerts, can we push to our pager duty?

[12:06] Alex: yes we support alerting to PagerDuty, Slack, and email integrations. Alert routing is per-route in the console.

[12:13] Maya: show one more thing — how do we do canary rollouts or A/B test models?

[12:19] Nina: console supports traffic splits by percentage and per-route selectors; you can do canary 5% to new model and ramp if metrics look good. it records token-level latencies so you can detect regressions quickly.

[12:35] [00:12:45] Alex: ok minute reminder — we'll send the security pack, example idempotency code, and a sandbox key. anything else from your side?

[12:46] Maya: do we need to sign an NDA to get security docs?

[12:49] Alex: security docs are available under NDA; sandbox credentials can be provided after the standard customer intake. we'll start the intake now.

[12:58] Jules: quick follow — are there any gotchas with embedding-based cache keys? we've seen collisions before.

[13:05] Nina: embedding collisions can happen; we threshold on similarity and use combined heuristics. mimic your actual paraphrase distribution in the bench to tune TTL.

[13:20] [00:13:30] Alex: final wrap — recap of next steps and action items. Nina, priya follow-up for stress test windows; alex will send sandbox and docs; nina will prepare benchmark script. customers will review security docs and confirm windows.

[13:40] Maya: thanks all, this was useful. we'll review and loop back with finance and infra.

[13:50] Alex: thanks — ending the recording.

End of transcript.
